kurals.tamil:
அலரெழ ஆருயிர் நிற்கும் அதனைப்
பலரறியார் பாக்கியத் தால்.
kurals.transliteration:
alarezha aaruyir niRkum adhanaip
palaraRiyaar paakkiyath thaal
kurals.meaning: Now that the town is gossiping about our love, my precious life, which was ebbing away, holds on; by good fortune the gossips do not realise that their talk is what keeps me alive.
kurals.elementary: Imagine you have a secret friend you are not allowed to play with, and you feel very sad. Then the other children start teasing, ‘You two are best friends!’ Strangely, the teasing makes you feel better, because now everyone treats you as a pair. The young man in this verse feels just like that, and he is glad the teasers have not worked out that they are helping him.
kurals.university: Chapter 115, alar aṟivuṟuttal (அலர் அறிவுறுத்தல்), concerns alar (அலர்) and its synonym kauvai (கௌவை), the village gossip that breaks out once a secret courtship (kaḷavu) becomes known; Parimelazhagar’s preface says the chapter has the hero telling the confidante (tōḻi) how the rumour serves him, and the heroine and tōḻi telling the hero of it to press him toward marriage (varaivu) or elopement (uṭanpōkku), and that it follows the chapter on abandoning reserve because it arises once nāṇ is given up. Parimelazhagar sets this couplet as the hero’s reply when the tōḻi, after a failed tryst, uses the rumour to urge marriage: the rumour makes the hard-to-win girl seem attainable, so his ‘precious life’ (ār uyir) has a support (paṟṟukkōṭu); pākkiyam (பாக்கியம்) is glossed teyvam, ‘fate, providence’, which keeps the gossips from realising this, for if they knew they would fall silent and his life would go. Manakkudavar instead reads ār uyir as the heroine’s life. The text is identical on ytamizh.com, thirukkural.net and thirukkural.com; Pope renders ‘By this same rumour’s rise, my precious life stands fast.’

hinduism.quote_or_event: The Gita Govinda opens with Nanda telling Radha to take Krishna home through the darkening forest, and the poem then follows the two lovers’ meeting by the Yamuna, away from the eyes of the village.
hinduism.explanation: Jayadeva’s poem treats Radha and Krishna’s love as something lived on the edge of village knowledge, half hidden and half known.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s lover lives in that same space, where a secret love becomes the talk of the village and the talk turns out to sustain it.
hinduism.source: Jayadeva, Gita Govinda, canto 1, opening verse (paraphrase)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known opening; it shares the setting of a love hidden from, then known to, the village, but Jayadeva never says gossip keeps the lover alive.

christianity.quote_or_event: When Joseph learns that Mary, to whom he is betrothed, is with child, he resolves to put her away privately rather than make her a public example.
christianity.explanation: Matthew shows a betrothed man weighing what public talk would do to the woman he is bound to.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural’s lover faces public talk about his beloved too, though for him the talk is welcome and keeps him alive.
christianity._accuracy_note: Paraphrase from memory of a familiar verse; it shares the theme of public talk about a betrothed couple but treats it as a threat to be avoided.

islam.quote_or_event: “And women in the city said, ‘The wife of al-ʿAzeez is seeking to seduce her slave boy; he has impassioned her with love. Indeed, we see her [to be] in clear error.’”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an records the gossip of the city’s women about Zulaikha’s love for Joseph.
islam.tie_back: This is the same alar, a love that has become the talk of the town, though here the gossip is pure censure and does nothing to sustain the lover.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via the quran.com API; a direct example of town gossip about love, but without the Kural’s twist that the gossip keeps the lover alive.

judaism.quote_or_event: “And she lay at his feet until the morning; and she rose up before one could discern another. For he said: ‘Let it not be known that the woman came to the threshing-floor.’”
judaism.explanation: Boaz takes care that his night meeting with Ruth does not become the talk of the town before he can marry her properly.
judaism.tie_back: Boaz fears exactly the alar the Kural’s lover welcomes, which shows how unusual the Tamil hero’s attitude is.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Sefaria; a genuine biblical concern with rumour about a courtship, but used here mostly as a contrast.

buddhism.quote_or_event: When rival wanderers spread a slanderous rumour about the Buddha after the murder of the wanderer Sundari, the monks are reviled in the town, and the Buddha tells them the noise will not last long and will vanish after seven days.
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha treats public talk as a passing noise that a calm mind can wait out.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural’s lover clings to the town’s talk as his lifeline; the Buddha teaches that such talk has no lasting power to give life or take it away.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known Udana episode; it is about scandalous rumour but the attitude to it is the opposite of the Kural’s.

jainism.quote_or_event: Jacobi’s note on the Kapila lecture retells the commentary story: the student Kapila fell in love with the servant girl who waited on him and, to buy her ornaments for a festival, set out at night to beg two pieces of gold, was arrested, and was brought before the king.
jainism.explanation: The Jain commentary uses a young man’s love affair, which ends in public exposure before the king, as the starting point of his conversion.
jainism.tie_back: Like the Kural’s hero, Kapila’s love is exposed to public view; the Jain tale, however, turns that exposure toward renunciation rather than marriage.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Lecture 8, Jacobi’s introductory note (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45) (paraphrase)
jainism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase checked against Jacobi’s note on sacred-texts.com; a genuine Jain story of a love made public, but it lacks the rumour-as-lifeline idea.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Hesiod warns that Talk (Pheme) is light and easily raised but hard to be rid of, and that talk voiced by many people never wholly dies away, for she too is in some way a goddess.
greek_mythology.explanation: For Hesiod, rumour is almost a divine power with a life of its own once many mouths carry it.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural’s lover experiences that self-sustaining life of rumour, but finds in it a power that keeps him alive rather than one to fear.
greek_mythology.source: Hesiod, Works and Days 760-764 (paraphrase; cf. tr. H.G. Evelyn-White)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known passage not rechecked this session; it shares the idea of rumour’s persistence, but Hesiod treats it as something to avoid.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Stendhal observes that a very small degree of hope is enough to give birth to love, and that love can then survive for a while on almost nothing.
philosophy.explanation: In De l’amour, love lives on hope, and even slight evidence can keep it alive.
philosophy.tie_back: The town’s rumour gives the Kural’s lover exactly that small hope, and it is enough to keep his life from slipping away.
philosophy.source: Stendhal, On Love (De l’amour, 1822), early chapters on the birth of love (paraphrase)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of Stendhal’s well-known account of hope in love, not rechecked word for word this session; a good psychological fit.

kurals.tamil:
மலரன்ன கண்ணாள் அருமை அறியாது
அலரெமக்கு ஈந்ததிவ் வூர்.
kurals.transliteration:
malaranna kaNNaaL arumai aRiyaadhu
alaremakku eendhadhiv voor
kurals.meaning: Not knowing how rare and hard to win is the girl with flower-like eyes, this town has handed me a rumour linking us, and so has done me a favour.
kurals.elementary: Suppose there is a very special girl in your class whom everyone thinks is out of reach. One day people start saying, ‘Oh, she likes you!’ They are only gossiping, but the gossip makes her seem a little closer. The young man in this verse thanks the town for gossiping, because the town has no idea how precious she really is.
kurals.university: Parimelazhagar marks this as ‘itu um atu’, the same situation as 1141, the hero speaking to the tōḻi. Arumai (அருமை) here means ‘difficulty of attainment’, which he explains as caused by failed trysts (alla kuṟi) and obstacles (iṭaiyīṭu); the town, unaware of it, has made her seem ‘easy’ (eḷiyaḷ) and so has ‘given’ (īntatu) him the rumour, a word chosen because the rumour is his support. Malar aṉṉa kaṇṇāḷ, ‘she whose eyes are like flowers’ (Puliyur Kesikan specifies the kuvaḷai or blue water-lily), is a conventional epithet. Manakkudavar reads arumai as the nobility of her birth (iṟpiṟappu), so that the gossips speak of her as of a common girl. The text agrees on ytamizh.com, thirukkural.net and thirukkural.com.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Uttara Kanda, Rama asks his companion Bhadra what the citizens are saying, and learns that the townspeople are gossiping about Sita, questioning how he could take her back after she lived in Ravana’s house.
hinduism.explanation: The people of Ayodhya talk about Sita without understanding her proven purity and worth.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural’s town, Ayodhya talks without knowing the true rarity of the woman it discusses, though in the Ramayana the gossip brings sorrow, not help.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a famous episode, not checked word for word this session; strong on ‘the town does not know her worth’, opposite in outcome.

christianity.quote_or_event: “My dove, my undefiled is but one; she is the only one of her mother, she is the choice one of her that bare her. The daughters saw her, and blessed her; yea, the queens and the concubines, and they praised her.”
christianity.explanation: The lover in the Song insists his beloved is unique, and pictures everyone who sees her recognising it.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural’s lover also knows his beloved is beyond compare; his complaint and his comfort is that the gossiping town has not seen it.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bolls.life KJV; matches the beloved’s rarity, while the public response here is praise rather than gossip.

islam.quote_or_event: “So when she heard of their scheming, she sent for them and prepared for them a banquet and gave each one of them a knife and said [to Joseph], ‘Come out before them.’ And when they saw him, they greatly admired him and cut their hands and said, ‘Perfect is Allāh! This is not a man; this is none but a noble angel.’”
islam.explanation: The women who gossiped about Zulaikha’s love change their tune the moment they see how extraordinary Joseph is.
islam.tie_back: This is exactly the Kural’s point: gossips talk about a love without knowing the rare worth of the beloved.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via the quran.com API (footnote markers removed); a close parallel of gossip that underrates the beloved, with the genders reversed.

judaism.quote_or_event: Proverbs asks who can find a woman of valour, and answers that her price is far above rubies.
judaism.explanation: The closing poem of Proverbs celebrates a woman whose worth is rare and hard to find.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural’s hero prizes his beloved for the same rarity (arumai) that the gossiping town fails to see.
judaism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known verse, not rechecked this session; it shares the theme of a rare woman’s worth, though it praises a wife rather than a beloved.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Dhammapada says that there never was, never will be and is not now anyone who is wholly blamed or wholly praised.
buddhism.explanation: The verse warns that public opinion is fickle and never a true measure of a person.
buddhism.tie_back: The town in the Kural misjudges the heroine’s worth, which illustrates exactly how unreliable public talk is.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a famous verse not rechecked this session; it fits the town’s misjudgment only in general terms.

jainism.quote_or_event: When Arishtanemi’s brother Rathanemi sees Rajimati alone and invites her to enjoy pleasures with him, she firmly rebukes him and recalls him to his monastic vows.
jainism.explanation: Rathanemi treats Rajimati as easily approachable and discovers her steadfastness and worth.
jainism.tie_back: Parimelazhagar says the gossips make the heroine seem ‘easy’ (eḷiyaḷ) without knowing her rarity; Rathanemi makes the same mistake about Rajimati.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Lecture 22 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45) (paraphrase)
jainism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known Jain episode not rechecked word for word this session; it fits misjudging a woman’s rarity but involves no town rumour.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: As Helen walks to the wall of Troy, the old men of the city murmur that it is no cause for blame that Trojans and Achaeans should suffer so long for such a woman, so like is she to the immortal goddesses, though they wish she would go home.
greek_mythology.explanation: The elders of Troy gossip about Helen, and in the same breath admit her extraordinary worth.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural’s town gossips without seeing the heroine’s rarity; Homer’s elders gossip and do see it.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a famous scene; a good picture of a town talking about a rare beauty, with the reverse twist that the talkers recognise her worth.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Montaigne argues that the judgment of the common crowd is too uncertain and ill-informed to be a measure of anyone’s true worth, and that a person should not live by it.
philosophy.explanation: In his essay on glory, Montaigne doubts that public reputation ever tracks real merit.
philosophy.tie_back: The gossiping town in the Kural proves his point by talking about a woman whose real value it has not grasped.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of the general argument of the essay, not rechecked this session; a general thematic fit only.

kurals.tamil:
உறாஅதோ ஊரறிந்த கௌவை அதனைப்
பெறாஅது பெற்றன்ன நீர்த்து.
kurals.transliteration:
uRaaadhoa ooraRindha keLavai adhanaip
peRaaadhu petranna neerththu
kurals.meaning: Is not the rumour the whole town knows a gain for me? Hearing it, my heart feels as if it already has the union it has not yet won.
kurals.elementary: Have you ever wanted a puppy so much that, when your friends started saying, ‘You’re getting a puppy!’, you felt almost as happy as if it were already sitting in your lap? The young man in this verse feels that way. The town’s talk about him and his beloved makes him feel as if they were already together.
kurals.university: Again ‘itu um atu’ in Parimelazhagar: the hero speaks. Uṟāatō (உறாஅதோ, with the alapeṭai lengthening) is a rhetorical question, ‘does it not come to me?’, and kauvai (கௌவை) is a synonym of alar; peṟāatu peṟṟaṉṉa nīrttu means ‘it has the nature of having got what was not got’. Parimelazhagar supplies maṉam, ‘my mind’, as the subject of nīrttu and glosses the phrase as having a joy like that of actual union. Manakkudavar reads it as the hero telling the tōḻi that the rumour should be welcomed, since through it the family will come to consent. The sources print கெளவை, which is a common encoding of கௌவை (kau) with separate vowel signs; this edition normalises it to கௌவை, as thirukkural.com’s Parimelazhagar text has it.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In Kalidasa’s Meghaduta, the exiled Yaksha, separated from his wife, consoles himself by picturing her in detail and sending a cloud as his messenger, as though contact could be had through imagination alone.
hinduism.explanation: The poem shows a lover living on an imagined closeness when the real one is denied.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s hero, too, enjoys through the town’s rumour a union he has not yet obtained.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of the poem’s overall situation; it shares the joy of imagined union, but the source of it is the lover’s fancy, not public rumour.

christianity.quote_or_event: The Letter to the Hebrews defines faith as the substance of things hoped for, the evidence of things not seen.
christianity.explanation: Faith, for the writer, makes what is hoped for present already in a real way.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural’s hero feels something similar: the rumour makes the union he hopes for feel already possessed.
christianity._accuracy_note: Paraphrase from memory of a familiar verse; only a structural parallel, since Hebrews speaks of religious faith, not love.

islam.quote_or_event: Ibn Hazm devotes a chapter of The Ring of the Dove to the lover’s contentment, describing how a lover separated from the beloved can be satisfied with very little, such as a glance, a token, or news of her.
islam.explanation: The Andalusian scholar sees that lovers make a feast out of the smallest share of the beloved.
islam.tie_back: The Kural’s hero is content in just this way: the mere rumour gives him the feeling of having what he does not have.
islam.source: Ibn Hazm, The Ring of the Dove (Tawq al-Hamama), chapter on contentment (paraphrase; cf. tr. A.J. Arberry)
islam._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a chapter theme in Ibn Hazm, not rechecked this session; a good psychological fit, though rumour is not named among the lover’s consolations.

judaism.quote_or_event: Jacob serves seven years for Rachel, and they seem to him but a few days, because of the love he has for her.
judaism.explanation: Love for Rachel makes the long wait feel short, as if the goal were already near.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural’s hero likewise feels the union he lacks as if it were already his, though for him it is rumour, not love alone, that does this.
judaism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a famous verse, not rechecked this session; it shares the sense of a not-yet-possessed love felt as near, with no element of rumour.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Buddha compares sensual pleasures to a dream: a man dreams of lovely parks and lakes, but on waking sees nothing of them.
buddhism.explanation: Pleasures enjoyed in the mind feel real but have no substance.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural’s hero enjoys a union that exists only in the town’s talk; Buddhism would call that pleasure dreamlike.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known simile, not rechecked this session; it matches ‘having as if had’ but evaluates it negatively.

jainism.quote_or_event: “A miracle! O king, you give up those wonderful pleasures, in search of imaginary objects; your very hope will cause your ruin.”
jainism.explanation: Indra, testing King Nami, accuses him of giving up real pleasures for imaginary ones; Nami answers that it is worldly pleasure that is the illusion.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural’s hero takes delight in a union that so far exists only in talk; the Jain dialogue asks which pleasures are real and which are imagined.
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com (Jacobi’s diacritics simplified); the theme of imagined possession is present, but the context is renunciation, not love.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Pygmalion falls in love with the ivory statue he has carved, treats it as if it were his living bride, and at last Venus brings it to life.
greek_mythology.explanation: Ovid’s sculptor lives as though he already had a beloved he does not yet truly have, until the wish is granted.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural’s hero, too, lives as if he already possessed the union that the rumour only promises.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a famous episode; it shares ‘having as if one had’, though Pygmalion’s illusion comes from art, not rumour.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Stendhal’s theory of crystallisation describes how the lover’s mind keeps adorning the beloved and imagining happiness with her, finding new perfections in every small piece of news.
philosophy.explanation: For Stendhal, imagination lets the lover enjoy a happiness that has not yet happened.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s hero crystallises around the town’s rumour, enjoying the union as if it were already his.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of Stendhal’s best-known idea, not rechecked word for word this session; a strong psychological fit.

kurals.tamil:
கவ்வையால் கவ்விது காமம் அதுவின்றேல்
தவ்வென்னும் தன்மை இழந்து.
kurals.transliteration:
kavvaiyaal kavvidhu kaamam adhuvindrael
thavvennum thanmai izhandhu
kurals.meaning: My love grows and blooms on the town’s gossip; without that gossip it would lose its nature and shrink away.
kurals.elementary: Think of a small campfire. If nobody adds sticks, it gets smaller and goes out. The town’s chatter is like sticks thrown on this young man’s love: every time people talk, his love burns brighter. Without the talk, he says, it would shrink like a fire nobody feeds.
kurals.university: Parimelazhagar again treats this as the hero’s speech. He explains the pun kavvaiyāl kavvitu: just as one says cevvitu of what has cevvai, the poet coins kavvitu, ‘full of kavvai’, and he glosses it as ‘has blossomed’ (alartal), with a play on alar, ‘rumour’, and alar, ‘to blossom’; the line means love ‘blossoms more and more’ on the rumour. Tavveṉṉum is an onomatopoeic expression (kuṟippu moḻi) for shrinking, which he supports with Neṭunalvāṭai 184-85. Its ‘nature’ (iyalpu) he defines as giving joy. Kavvai here is a variant form of kauvai, used for the pun; all three sources print the same text.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Krishna traces how desire grows: by dwelling on sense objects a person becomes attached to them, from attachment desire is born, and from desire anger arises.
hinduism.explanation: The Gita describes desire as something that feeds on attention and grows step by step.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s hero describes his love growing in just this way, fed by the constant attention of the town’s talk.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 2.62 (paraphrase; cf. tr. Swami Mukundananda)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a famous verse, not rechecked word for word this session; it shares the mechanism of desire growing by attention, but the Gita condemns it.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Even so the tongue is a little member, and boasteth great things. Behold, how great a matter a little fire kindleth!”
christianity.explanation: James warns that a little talk can set a great blaze going.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural’s hero describes just this: the town’s small talk has kindled his love into something far larger.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bolls.life KJV; the image of talk as fuel fits well, but James warns against it.

islam.quote_or_event: Ibn Hazm gives separate chapters of The Ring of the Dove to the figures who surround lovers, among them the reproacher who blames the lover and the slanderer who spreads talk, and he describes how lovers are affected by them.
islam.explanation: The Andalusian treatise treats gossip and reproach as forces that shape the course of a love affair.
islam.tie_back: The Kural’s hero says the same: the town’s talk does not stay outside his love but makes it grow.
islam.source: Ibn Hazm, The Ring of the Dove (Tawq al-Hamama), chapters on the reproacher and the slanderer (paraphrase; cf. tr. A.J. Arberry)
islam._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of chapter themes, not rechecked this session; Ibn Hazm treats talk as an affliction more than as a nourishment.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Where no wood is, the fire goeth out; And where there is no whisperer, contention ceaseth.”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs observes that whispering keeps a quarrel alive, just as wood keeps a fire burning.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural applies the same logic to love: without the town’s whispering, the hero says, his love would die down.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Sefaria; a close structural match (talk as fuel), though Proverbs speaks of strife rather than love.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “The craving of one given to heedless living grows like a creeper.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada compares craving to a creeper that keeps spreading as long as it is fed.
buddhism.tie_back: Kalaignar glosses this kural with the image of a love-creeper (kātalkoṭi) that withers without the town’s talk; the Buddha uses the same image for craving that keeps growing.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Access to Insight (first sentence of the verse); same image of growth, opposite valuation.

jainism.quote_or_event: “If there were numberless mountains of gold and silver, as big as Kailâsa, they would not satisfy a greedy man; for his avidity is boundless like space.”
jainism.explanation: Nami teaches that craving has no natural limit and grows without end.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural’s hero describes a love that keeps growing as long as it is fed; Jainism sees that endless growth as the mark of craving.
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; shares the idea of desire that grows without limit, but concerns greed rather than love or rumour.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In a myth retold by the orator Themistius, the child Eros would not grow until Aphrodite gave birth to his brother Anteros, ‘returned love’; with Anteros beside him Eros grew, and without him he shrank again.
greek_mythology.explanation: The myth says love needs something outside itself to feed it, or it stays small.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural’s hero says his love likewise needs the town’s talk to grow, and without it would shrink.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a late-antique myth, not rechecked this session; strong on ‘love shrinks without nourishment’, though the nourishment is returned love, not gossip.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Spinoza argues that if we imagine others love, desire or hate the same thing we love, desire or hate, we will love, desire or hate it more steadily.
philosophy.explanation: Our feelings, for Spinoza, are strengthened when we see them reflected in others.
philosophy.tie_back: The town’s talk reflects the hero’s love back to him, and by Spinoza’s logic this makes it stronger.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of the proposition, not rechecked word for word this session; a good mechanism for the Kural’s claim, though Spinoza speaks of shared feeling rather than gossip.

kurals.tamil:
களித்தொறும் கள்ளுண்டல் வேட்டற்றால் காமம்
வெளிப்படுந் தோறும் இனிது.
kurals.transliteration:
kaLiththoRum kaLLuNdal vaettatraal kaamam
veLippatunh thoaRum inidhu
kurals.meaning: Just as a drinker wants more toddy each time it makes him merry, my love grows sweeter each time it is made public by the rumour.
kurals.elementary: Some sweets are so tasty that each one makes you want another. The young man says his love is like that. Each time people talk about it, it feels sweeter, and he wants it talked about even more.
kurals.university: Parimelazhagar again gives this to the hero and explains vēṭṭaṟṟāl as a shortened form of vēṭkappaṭṭaṟṟāl, ‘as it is desired’: for drinkers, drinking toddy (kaḷ) grows sweeter each time they become merry (kaḷittoṟum), and so the hero’s love grows sweeter each time it is made known (veḷippaṭuntoṟum) by rumour. His point is that the very strength of desire makes even scandal pleasant. Manakkudavar assigns the couplet differently, to the tōḻi answering a hero who asked whether the rumour distressed them. The simile is striking given that chapter 93, kaḷḷuṇṇāmai, condemns drink; here the image describes the lover’s state without endorsing drinking. The text agrees in all three sources.

hinduism.quote_or_event: King Yayati, after a thousand years of enjoyment regained through his son’s youth, declares that desire is never satisfied by enjoying its objects but only blazes higher, like fire fed with clarified butter, and returns his son’s youth.
hinduism.explanation: The Mahabharata uses Yayati to show that every indulgence of desire makes it want more.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s drinker wants more with each cup, and its lover finds love sweeter each time it is talked about; Yayati is the classic Indian picture of that endless appetite.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Adi Parva, Sambhava Parva, story of Yayati (paraphrase; cf. tr. K.M. Ganguli)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of Yayati’s famous lesson, not rechecked against Ganguli this session; a strong fit for the self-feeding nature of desire.

christianity.quote_or_event: “They have stricken me, shalt thou say, and I was not sick; they have beaten me, and I felt it not: when shall I awake? I will seek it yet again.”
christianity.explanation: Proverbs portrays a drunkard who, in spite of every harm, only wants another drink.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural uses the same picture of the drinker who wants more, applying it to a lover who wants his love talked about more and more.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bolls.life KJV; the drinker’s craving matches the Kural’s simile closely, though Proverbs uses it as a warning.

islam.quote_or_event: Ibn al-Farid’s Wine Ode opens with the lovers drinking, in remembrance of the Beloved, a wine with which they were drunk before the vine was created.
islam.explanation: The Sufi poet makes intoxication the image of a love that is endlessly sweet and never sated.
islam.tie_back: The Kural, too, makes drinking the image of love that becomes sweeter the more it is tasted and revealed.
islam.source: Ibn al-Farid, al-Khamriyya (The Wine Ode), opening verse (paraphrase; cf. tr. A.J. Arberry)
islam._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a famous opening, not rechecked against a translation this session; same image of love as wine, though the love is mystical.

judaism.quote_or_event: The Song of Songs opens with the beloved saying that her lover’s love is better than wine.
judaism.explanation: The Song compares love and wine and finds love the sweeter.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural, too, sets love beside drink and finds that love, made public, grows ever sweeter.
judaism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known verse, not rechecked this session; same pairing of love and wine, without the element of public talk.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Buddha describes a leper who scratches his sores and burns them over a pit of coals; the more he does it, the worse his wounds become, yet he finds a kind of pleasure in it.
buddhism.explanation: Sensual desire, says the Buddha, feeds on what makes it worse and is mistaken for pleasure.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural’s drinker and lover both find sweetness in what only increases their craving; the Buddha calls that the leper’s pleasure.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known simile, not rechecked word for word this session; a strong structural match with an opposite judgment.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Pleasures are the thorn that rankles, pleasures are poison, pleasures are like a venomous snake; he who is desirous of pleasures will not get them, and will come to a bad end at last.”
jainism.explanation: Nami teaches that the sweetness of pleasure is a trap that leads to more craving and suffering.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural’s lover finds love sweeter each time it is revealed, just as the drinker finds drink sweeter; Jainism warns that this growing sweetness is the poison itself.
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; a genuine Jain teaching on the sweetness of pleasure, but it speaks against the Kural’s celebration of it.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Odysseus’ men who taste the lotus lose all wish to return home and want only to stay among the Lotus-eaters, eating more of it.
greek_mythology.explanation: Homer’s lotus is sweet in a way that makes people want nothing but more of it.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural’s drinker and lover are caught by the same sweetness, which grows the more it is tasted.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a famous episode; a fair image of self-feeding sweetness, without any connection to love.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Lucretius says that love is the one thing of which the more we have, the more fiercely the heart burns with desire.
philosophy.explanation: For Lucretius, love is unlike hunger or thirst, which are satisfied; possessing more of it only makes the craving stronger.
philosophy.tie_back: This is the logic of the Kural’s drinker: each taste makes the next one more wanted, and love revealed grows sweeter.
philosophy.source: Lucretius, De Rerum Natura 4.1088-1090 (paraphrase; cf. tr. W.H.D. Rouse)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a famous passage, not rechecked against a translation this session; a close match for the self-increasing appetite of love.

kurals.tamil:
கண்டது மன்னும் ஒருநாள் அலர்மன்னும்
திங்களைப் பாம்புகொண் டற்று.
kurals.transliteration:
kaNdadhu mannum orunhaaL alarmannum
thingaLaip paampukoN tatru
kurals.meaning: I saw my beloved only once, yet the rumour of it has spread everywhere, like the news when the serpent swallows the moon.
kurals.elementary: When there is an eclipse and the moon goes dark, everybody in the whole town talks about it at once. The girl in this verse says she met her sweetheart just one single time, and now the whole town is talking about them, as if it were an eclipse!
kurals.university: Here the speaker changes. Parimelazhagar says the heroine, kept from the hero by obstacles and failed trysts, speaks to the tōḻi while the hero is within earshot (ciṟaippuṟam), announcing the rumour to press him to marry. Kaṇṭatu ‘what I saw’ took place ‘on one day’ (orunāḷ), but the alar is ‘like the serpent seizing the moon’ (tiṅkaḷaip pāmpu koṇṭaṟṟu), the eclipse caused by Rāhu that everyone sees and talks about; Parimelazhagar notes that the effect (the universal talk) is described by naming the cause, and that both maṉṉum and the um are expletives (acai nilai). His moral is that a love that draws rumour even without meetings cannot go on, and must end in marriage. Kalaignar glosses the image explicitly as the eclipse (kirakaṇam).

hinduism.quote_or_event: “And from that time there is a long-standing quarrel between Rahu’s head and Surya and Soma. And to this day it swalloweth Surya and Soma (during solar and lunar eclipses).”
hinduism.explanation: The Mahabharata tells how the demon Rahu was beheaded for tasting the nectar of immortality and ever since swallows the sun and moon at eclipses.
hinduism.tie_back: This is the myth behind the Kural’s image of the serpent seizing the moon, an event the whole world sees at once, just as the whole town hears of the lovers’ single meeting.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Adi Parva, Section 19 (Astika Parva) (tr. K.M. Ganguli)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; it explains the Kural’s eclipse image exactly, though it does not concern rumour or love.

christianity.quote_or_event: After Jesus heals a leper and tells him to say nothing, the man goes out and begins to spread the story everywhere, so that Jesus can no longer openly enter a city.
christianity.explanation: A single private event becomes, through one man’s telling, the talk of the whole region.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine experiences the same thing: one private meeting becomes the talk of the whole town.
christianity._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a familiar passage, not rechecked this session; a good fit for a single event spreading everywhere, in a non-romantic context.

islam.quote_or_event: “When you received it with your tongues and said with your mouths that of which you had no knowledge and thought it was insignificant while it was, in the sight of Allāh, tremendous.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an describes, in the setting of the slander against Aisha, how a rumour passes from tongue to tongue among people who know nothing of the truth.
islam.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine sees the same mechanism: a rumour about one meeting passes from mouth to mouth until it is everywhere.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via the quran.com API (footnote marker removed); it describes how rumour spreads, while condemning it.

judaism.quote_or_event: The Talmud teaches that an eclipse of the moon is a bad omen, a sign seen and feared by all the world.
judaism.explanation: For the rabbis an eclipse is a public event that everybody notices and interprets.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural also uses the eclipse as the image of something everyone sees and talks about at once.
judaism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a known passage, not rechecked this session; it shares the eclipse image only, without the theme of rumour.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Now at that time the Moon God had been seized by Rāhu, lord of titans.”
buddhism.explanation: The Moon God, seized by Rahu, calls on the Buddha for refuge, and Rahu releases him.
buddhism.tie_back: This is the same eclipse image the Kural uses for a rumour that spreads everywhere at once.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on SuttaCentral; it shares the precise image of Rahu seizing the moon, but has nothing to do with rumour.

jainism.quote_or_event: “When the royal Seer Nami retired from the world, at the occasion of his Pravragyâ there was an uproar in Mithilâ.”
jainism.explanation: Nami’s single act of renunciation sets the whole city of Mithila talking and crying out.
jainism.tie_back: Like the Kural’s single meeting, one event in one life becomes, in a moment, the noise of an entire city.
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com (diacritics kept); a genuine Jain picture of one act becoming a city’s uproar, though the event is renunciation, not love.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: After Dido and Aeneas shelter together in a cave during a storm, Rumour (Fama), the swiftest of all evils, races through the great cities of Libya spreading the story of their love.
greek_mythology.explanation: Virgil personifies Rumour as a monster that grows as it travels, with as many tongues as feathers.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This is almost exactly the Kural: one meeting, and at once the rumour of it is everywhere.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a famous passage, not rechecked against a translation this session; a near one-to-one match of a single meeting turned into universal rumour.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Francis Bacon, in his unfinished essay ‘Of Fame’, takes up the poets’ picture of Fame as a monster with many feathers, eyes and tongues, and asks how rumours arise and spread.
philosophy.explanation: Bacon treats rumour as a force worth studying, with its own ways of growing and travelling.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine has seen how fast such a monster runs: one meeting, and the whole town knows.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of the essay’s opening theme, not rechecked this session; a general fit on how rumour spreads.

kurals.tamil:
ஊரவர் கௌவை எருவாக அன்னைசொல்
நீராக நீளும்இந் நோய்.
kurals.transliteration:
ooravar kavai eruvaaka annaisol
neeraaka neeLum-inh noai
kurals.meaning: This lovesickness grows like a crop, with the town’s gossip as its manure and my mother’s angry words as its water.
kurals.elementary: A farmer puts manure on a plant and waters it, and the plant grows tall. The girl in this verse says the town’s gossip is like manure for her love, and her mother’s scolding is like water. Instead of stopping her love, they make it grow bigger and bigger.
kurals.university: Parimelazhagar sets this in a later situation: the marriage is delayed, the heroine is suffering, and the tōḻi, knowing the hero is within earshot, tells her to bear up in view of the town’s talk and her mother’s words; this is her reply. Nōy (நோய்), ‘illness’, is the love-sickness, imagined as a crop (payir) through a partial metaphor (ēkatēca uruvakam): ūravar kauvai, the talk of the town’s women (he notes ūravar here excludes men, by what they do), is eru (எரு), ‘manure’, and aṉṉai col, the mother’s angry words (veñcol), is nīr, ‘water’, so it nīḷum, ‘keeps growing’. His comment is that the very things that should have made it shrink make it spread, and the intended effect is that the hero will marry. The sources print கெளவை for kauvai and the sandhi-joined நீளும்இந்; the reading is otherwise unvaried.

hinduism.quote_or_event: When the gopis hear Krishna’s flute at night, they leave at once, and though husbands, fathers and brothers try to stop them, they cannot be held back.
hinduism.explanation: The Bhagavata shows family opposition doing nothing to check the gopis’ love for Krishna.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine finds the same: her family’s scolding only makes her love grow stronger.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a famous passage, not rechecked this session; a good fit for family opposition failing to stop love, though the love is devotional.

christianity.quote_or_event: In the parable of the barren fig tree, the gardener begs for one more year so that he may dig about the tree and dung it, in the hope that it will bear fruit.
christianity.explanation: Jesus uses the familiar work of manuring a plant to speak about growth given a last chance.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural uses the same farming image of manure making a plant grow, but the ‘plant’ is love and the ‘manure’ is gossip.
christianity._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a familiar parable, not rechecked this session; it shares only the image of manuring a plant.

islam.quote_or_event: In Nizami’s Layla and Majnun, when talk of the two young lovers spreads, Layla’s family takes her out of school and keeps her shut up at home, and the separation only makes Qays’s love burn more fiercely until he is called Majnun.
islam.explanation: Family restriction and public talk, meant to end the love, only deepen it.
islam.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine says the same: town talk and her mother’s words make her love grow, not die.
islam._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of the well-known narrative; a strong fit for opposition feeding love, though Nizami’s focus is on the young man.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Look not upon me, that I am swarthy, That the sun hath tanned me; My mother’s sons were incensed against me, They made me keeper of the vineyards; But mine own vineyard have I not kept.”
judaism.explanation: The beloved in the Song complains that her own family was angry with her and set her to work, yet she did not keep her own ‘vineyard’, her own heart.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine also faces anger at home, and like the Song’s beloved her love grows in spite of it.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Sefaria (outer quotation marks removed); family anger is present, but it is her brothers rather than her mother.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Whoever is overcome by this wretched and sticky craving, his sorrows grow like grass after the rains.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada pictures sorrow growing from craving like grass that has been watered.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural pictures love-sickness growing like a watered crop; the Buddha uses the same farming image for craving and its sorrows.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Access to Insight; a close match of the watered-growth image, from the opposite point of view.

jainism.quote_or_event: In Hemachandra’s account, the young Jambu’s parents arrange his marriage to eight brides to hold him back from renunciation, but their pleading on the wedding night only strengthens his resolve, and he converts them instead.
jainism.explanation: The family’s efforts to turn Jambu from his chosen path end up confirming it.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine also finds that her mother’s opposition only strengthens what it was meant to stop, though her path is love, not renunciation.
jainism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known Jain narrative, not checked against a translation this session; a structural parallel only.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In the tale of Cupid and Psyche, Venus, Cupid’s mother, is furious at her son’s love for a mortal girl, scolds him harshly and persecutes Psyche, yet their love endures and ends in marriage.
greek_mythology.explanation: A mother’s anger, meant to break a love, cannot destroy it.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine says her mother’s angry words water her love rather than kill it.
greek_mythology.source: Apuleius, Metamorphoses (The Golden Ass) 4-6 (Cupid and Psyche) (paraphrase)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a famous tale; a good fit for maternal anger failing to end love, though it is the lover’s mother, not the heroine’s.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Hume observes that opposition and difficulty, instead of weakening a passion, often rouse the spirits and give the passion more force.
philosophy.explanation: For Hume, obstacles can intensify the feelings they seem to oppose.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine describes exactly this: the town’s talk and her mother’s words make her love stronger.
philosophy.source: David Hume, A Treatise of Human Nature 2.3.4 (paraphrase)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of Hume’s discussion of what increases the passions, not rechecked against the text this session; the general point fits well.

kurals.tamil:
நெய்யால் எரிநுதுப்பேம் என்றற்றால் கௌவையால்
காமம் நுதுப்பேம் எனல்.
kurals.transliteration:
neyyaal erinhudhuppaem endratraal kavvaiyaal
Kaamam nudhuppeam enal
kurals.meaning: To think that gossip can put out love is like thinking you can put out a fire by pouring ghee on it.
kurals.elementary: If you pour water on a fire, it goes out. But if you pour oil or butter on it, it flares up even higher! The girl in this verse says people who try to stop love by gossiping are making the same mistake: they are pouring butter on the fire.
kurals.university: Parimelazhagar marks this ‘itu um atu’, continuing the heroine’s speech of 1147. Nutuppēm (நுதுப்பேம்) means ‘we shall extinguish’; ney (நெய்), ‘ghee, clarified butter’, is the classic accelerant of the sacrificial fire. He notes that the third-case endings (-āl) are instrumental and sums up: love cannot be extinguished by rumour, which is the very cause of its flaring up. Manakkudavar assigns the couplet to the tōḻi, speaking when the hero still wants to continue the secret affair. The comparison of desire to fire fed with ghee is widespread in Indian literature, notably in Manu and in the story of Yayati, which gives this couplet unusually direct parallels. The text agrees in all three sources apart from the கெளவை spelling, normalised here.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Desire is never extinguished by the enjoyment of desired objects; it only grows stronger like a fire (fed) with clarified butter.”
hinduism.explanation: Manu uses the image of ghee poured on fire to show that feeding desire only makes it burn hotter.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural uses the very same image: trying to put out love with gossip is like trying to put out fire with ghee.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; the same fire-and-ghee image, though Manu speaks of enjoyment feeding desire, while the Kural speaks of gossip.

christianity.quote_or_event: “But sin, taking occasion by the commandment, wrought in me all manner of concupiscence. For without the law sin was dead.”
christianity.explanation: Paul observes that a prohibition, instead of killing desire, can stir it up.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural says the same of gossip: what was meant to stifle love only inflames it.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bolls.life KJV; a strong structural match (opposition feeding desire), though Paul is speaking about sin and the law.

islam.quote_or_event: In Nizami’s Layla and Majnun, Majnun’s father takes him to the Kaaba to pray to be cured of his love, but Majnun instead prays that his love may grow ever stronger.
islam.explanation: The attempt to extinguish Majnun’s love only makes him ask for more of it.
islam.tie_back: This is the Kural’s point dramatised: efforts to put out love become fuel for it.
islam.source: Nizami Ganjavi, Layla and Majnun (1188), the pilgrimage to Mecca (paraphrase)
islam._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a famous episode of the narrative; a strong fit, though the agent is a father’s prayer rather than public gossip.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Many waters cannot quench love, Neither can the floods drown it; If a man would give all the substance of his house for love, He would utterly be contemned.”
judaism.explanation: The Song of Songs insists that nothing outside love can put it out.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural says the same with a sharper image: not water but ghee, gossip that only feeds the flame.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Sefaria; a near match on love that cannot be quenched, though the Song does not say the quenching attempt feeds it.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Fire Sermon the Buddha declares that the eye, its objects and everything experienced through the senses are burning, burning with the fire of passion, aversion and delusion.
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha pictures sensual life as a fire that keeps burning on what the senses feed it.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural, too, sees love as a fire that the town’s gossip only feeds; the Buddha’s remedy is to stop feeding it altogether.
buddhism.source: Samyutta Nikaya 35.28 (Adittapariyaya Sutta, the Fire Sermon) (paraphrase)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a famous sutta, not rechecked this session; same fire image, opposite valuation.

jainism.quote_or_event: “The more you get, the more you want; your desires increase with your means. Though two mâshas would do to supply your want, still you would scarcely think ten millions sufficient.”
jainism.explanation: Kapila, who began by wanting two pieces of gold for the girl he loved, discovers that each satisfaction only enlarges desire.
jainism.tie_back: Like ghee poured on fire, what was meant to satisfy Kapila’s love-driven wish only made it blaze higher, which is the Kural’s point about love.
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; a strong match for desire fed rather than quenched, rooted in a love story, though the fuel is wealth rather than gossip.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Ovid’s Pyramus and Thisbe are forbidden by their fathers to marry, but the prohibition cannot stop their love: the more it is covered up, the more the hidden fire burns.
greek_mythology.explanation: Parental prohibition and concealment only make the young lovers’ passion fiercer.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural says the same of gossip: what is meant to put out love only makes it burn harder.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a famous passage, not rechecked against a translation this session; the fire image and the failure of opposition both match.

philosophy.quote_or_event: La Rochefoucauld writes that absence lessens moderate passions and increases great ones, as the wind blows out candles and fans a fire.
philosophy.explanation: The same obstacle can extinguish a small feeling and inflame a great one.
philosophy.tie_back: The town’s gossip is such a wind: on the Kural’s great love it acts like fuel on a fire, not like a breath on a candle.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a famous maxim (number as commonly given, not rechecked this session); same fire image, with absence rather than gossip as the obstacle.

kurals.tamil:
அலர்நாண ஒல்வதோ அஞ்சலோம்பு என்றார்
பலர்நாண நீத்தக் கடை.
kurals.transliteration:
alarnhaaNa olvadhoa anjaloambu endraar
palarnhaaNa neeththak kadai
kurals.meaning: He once told me, ‘Do not be afraid,’ and now he has left me in a way that shames me before many; how can I still be ashamed of the town’s gossip?
kurals.elementary: Imagine a friend promised, ‘Don’t worry, I’ll always stay with you,’ and then went away, so everyone could see you were left alone. You might think, ‘Everyone already knows I’ve been left. Why should I be embarrassed about what they say now?’ That is how the girl in this verse feels.
kurals.university: Parimelazhagar sets this when the hero has gone away, leaving the marriage still pending; the heroine, aware he has returned and is within earshot, answers the tōḻi who told her to endure for fear of the rumour. Añcal ōmpu (அஞ்சல் ஓம்பு), ‘guard against fear, do not fear’, recalls the hero’s promise at their first meeting, ‘I will not leave you’; now he has abandoned her ‘so that the many are ashamed’ (palar nāṇa), and she asks whether she can still feel nāṇ before alar. He paraphrases her meaning: ‘We, who are in a state that makes onlookers blush, where is our shame?’ Manakkudavar takes the ‘many’ as the tōḻi, the foster-mother (cevili) and the household. Solomon Pappaiah’s gloss reads the line differently, as the hero having said ‘fear not’ even as he departed; the text itself agrees in all three sources.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Mirabai sings that she has thrown away the shame of the world (lok-laj): her family scolds her and people call her mad, but she will not hide her love for Krishna.
hinduism.explanation: The bhakti poet makes indifference to public shame a sign of a love that has gone beyond caring what people say.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine reaches the same point: having been left before everyone, she can no longer be ashamed of their gossip.
hinduism.source: Mirabai, padas (paraphrase; cf. tr. A.J. Alston, The Devotional Poems of Mirabai)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a recurring theme in Mirabai’s songs, not tied to one checked verse; a strong fit for giving up shame before public talk.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Peter said unto him, Though I should die with thee, yet will I not deny thee. Likewise also said all the disciples.” Later that night: “Then all the disciples forsook him, and fled.”
christianity.explanation: Those who promised never to abandon Jesus leave him at the moment of public shame.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine has suffered the same: the one who promised ‘fear not’ has left her exposed before everyone.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bolls.life KJV; strong on a promise of faithfulness broken in public, but the relationship is not romantic.

islam.quote_or_event: Al-Hujwiri describes the Malamatiyya, the ‘people of blame’, Sufis who deliberately accept people’s reproach so that public opinion has no hold on their love for God.
islam.explanation: For these Sufis, being freed from concern about blame is part of loving sincerely.
islam.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine, abandoned in public, also reaches the point where the town’s blame can no longer shame her.
islam.source: Al-Hujwiri, Kashf al-Mahjub, chapter on blame (malama) (paraphrase; cf. tr. R.A. Nicholson)
islam._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known Sufi doctrine, not rechecked against Nicholson this session; it shares indifference to blame, though chosen rather than forced on her.

judaism.quote_or_event: Lamentations pictures Jerusalem as a woman weeping in the night, who among all her lovers has none to comfort her, for all her friends have dealt treacherously with her.
judaism.explanation: The city is portrayed as a woman abandoned by those who had pledged themselves to her, exposed before the nations.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine is likewise abandoned by the one who promised to stay, and left exposed before everyone.
judaism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known verse, not rechecked this session; strong on abandonment and public shame, though the speaker is a personified city.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Just as a solid rock is not shaken by the storm, even so the wise are not affected by praise or blame.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha teaches that the wise person stands firm whatever others say.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine also stops being shaken by blame, though out of grief rather than wisdom.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Access to Insight; same result (indifference to blame) from a very different cause.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Happy are we, happy live we who call nothing our own; when Mithilâ is on fire, nothing is burned that belongs to me.”
jainism.explanation: Nami, having let go of everything, is untouched by the uproar and fire in his city.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine, having lost what mattered most, is likewise beyond being hurt by the town’s talk, though she has not chosen that loss as Nami did.
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; shares an indifference to public clamour, but it springs from renunciation, not abandonment.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Ovid’s Heroides, Ariadne, abandoned on the island of Naxos by Theseus after she saved him, writes reproaching him for the promises he made and for leaving her alone and disgraced.
greek_mythology.explanation: Ariadne is the classic figure of the woman abandoned by the man who swore to protect her.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine has suffered the same broken promise of ‘do not fear’, and the same public exposure.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a famous letter; a strong fit for promise and abandonment, though Ariadne does not reflect on rumour.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Epictetus advises that if someone tells you a person has spoken ill of you, you should not defend yourself, but answer that he must not have known your other faults, or he would have mentioned them too.
philosophy.explanation: For the Stoic, other people’s talk is outside our control and should not disturb us.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine also refuses to be ashamed of the town’s talk, though from grief rather than Stoic calm.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known saying, not rechecked this session; same refusal to be shamed by talk, different motive.

kurals.tamil:
தாம்வேண்டின் நல்குவர் காதலர் யாம்வேண்டும்
கௌவை எடுக்கும்இவ் வூர்.
kurals.transliteration:
thaamvaeNtin nalkuvar kaadhalar yaamvaendum
kavvai edukkum-iv voor
kurals.meaning: The town is now raising just the rumour we wanted; so if we ask him, our lover will gladly agree to what we want.
kurals.elementary: Imagine you have been hoping your parents will let you go on a trip with your best friend. Then everybody starts saying, ‘Those two always go everywhere together!’ The talk makes the trip seem natural, and you feel sure your friend will say yes when you ask. That is how the girl’s friend feels in this verse.
kurals.university: In Parimelazhagar’s reading the speaker is now the tōḻi, addressing the heroine while the hero is within earshot, to make him favour elopement (uṭaṉpōkku). ‘The rumour we have long wanted’ (yām vēṇṭum kauvai), wanted because it gives a reason for leaving together, ‘the town itself is raising’ (eṭukkum); kātalar, ‘the lover’, chosen to suggest that because he loves her he will not refuse, ‘will grant it if we ask’ (tām vēṇṭiṉ nalkuvar). He closes his commentary by noting that the twenty couplets of chapters 114 and 115 are all puṇartal nimittam, occasions leading toward union. Manakkudavar reads the second clause differently, that the family will now themselves agree to give her to the lover; modern glosses (Pappaiah: he will marry me; Varadarasanar: he will grant it) vary between marriage and elopement.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Rukmini, whose brother has promised her to Shishupala, sends a brahmin with a letter asking Krishna to come and carry her away; Krishna agrees at once and takes her from the temple before the wedding.
hinduism.explanation: The Bhagavata tells of a woman who asks her beloved to take her away against her family’s plans, and of the lover who readily consents.
hinduism.tie_back: The tōḻi in the Kural is sure the lover will agree to take the heroine away if asked, just as Krishna answers Rukmini.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a famous episode, not rechecked this session; a close match for a requested elopement readily granted.

christianity.quote_or_event: “My beloved spake, and said unto me, Rise up, my love, my fair one, and come away.”
christianity.explanation: The lover in the Song invites the beloved to leave with him.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural’s tōḻi expects the lover to give just such an invitation now that the town’s talk has made the way clear.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bolls.life KJV; a close match for the invitation to go away together, without the element of rumour.

islam.quote_or_event: Ibn Ishaq relates that Khadija, admiring Muhammad’s character, sent word through an intermediary proposing marriage, and he accepted.
islam.explanation: In this account the woman takes the initiative, confident her proposal will be welcomed, and it is.
islam.tie_back: The Kural’s tōḻi is likewise confident the lover will grant what the heroine asks, now that the town has made their bond known.
islam.source: Ibn Ishaq, Sirat Rasul Allah, marriage of Khadija (paraphrase; cf. tr. A. Guillaume)
islam._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known account, not rechecked this session; it shares the woman’s initiative and the man’s ready consent, but there is no rumour or elopement.

judaism.quote_or_event: When Abraham’s servant asks to take Rebekah to Isaac, her family say they will call the girl and ask her, and when asked whether she will go with this man, she answers, I will go.
judaism.explanation: Rebekah consents to leave her home and go to the man she is to marry.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural, too, turns on a question of consent to leave home, with the tōḻi sure the answer will be yes.
judaism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a famous passage, not rechecked this session; a good fit for consent to leave with a bridegroom, though not an elopement.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Pali commentaries tell that Patacara, a rich man’s daughter, fell in love with a family servant, and when her parents arranged another marriage she ran away with him to live in a distant village.
buddhism.explanation: Patacara’s story is a Buddhist account of an elopement, which later ends in tragedy and her conversion.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural’s tōḻi is urging exactly such an elopement (uṭaṉpōkku), though the Buddhist story shows where its sorrows can lead.
buddhism.source: Therigatha commentary and Dhammapada commentary, story of Patacara (paraphrase)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known commentarial story; a genuine elopement parallel, though without the rumour and with a tragic outcome.

jainism.quote_or_event: When Arishtanemi leaves his wedding to become a monk, Rajimati, his bride, resolves to follow him, takes the vows herself, and goes to the mountain where he is practising austerities.
jainism.explanation: In the Jain story the bride follows the man she loves, but into renunciation rather than married life.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine is urged to follow her lover away from home; Rajimati also follows hers, though to a very different end.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Lecture 22 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45) (paraphrase)
jainism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known Jain narrative, not rechecked word for word this session; a genuine ‘following the beloved’ story, turned toward renunciation.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Medea, having helped Jason win the Golden Fleece, flees her father’s house by night and sails away with him, after he swears to make her his wedded wife.
greek_mythology.explanation: The Argonautica tells one of the classic elopements of Greek myth.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural’s tōḻi hopes for just such a flight with the lover, now that the rumour has made it seem natural.
greek_mythology.source: Apollonius of Rhodes, Argonautica 4 (paraphrase; cf. tr. R.C. Seaton)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a famous episode; a genuine elopement parallel, though driven by danger rather than rumour.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In Plato’s Phaedrus, the beloved, receiving the lover’s affection, comes to feel a returning love (anteros), an image of the lover’s own, and begins to desire his company in turn.
philosophy.explanation: Plato describes how love, once shown, awakens an answering love in the beloved.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s tōḻi trusts that the lover’s own love (he is kātalar, ‘the one who loves’) will make him agree to what the heroine asks.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known passage, not rechecked this session; a general fit on returned love, without rumour or elopement.
